original_abstract: Omnidirectional scene text detection has received increasing research attention. Previous methods directly predict words or text lines of quadrilateral shapes. However, most methods neglect the significance of consistent labeling, which is important to maintain a stable training process, especially when a large amount of data are included. For the first time, we solve the problem in this paper by proposing a novel method termed Sequential-free Box Discretization (SBD). The proposed SBD first discretizes the quadrilateral box into several key edges, which contains all potential horizontal and vertical positions. In order to decode accurate vertex positions, a simple yet effective matching procedure is proposed to reconstruct the quadrilateral bounding boxes. It departs from the learning ambiguity which has a significant influence during the learning process. Exhaustive ablation studies have been conducted to quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, built upon SBD, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of a collection of refinements, in the hope to inspire others to build state-of-the-art networks. Combining both SBD and these useful refinements, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including ICDAR 2015, and MLT. Our method also wins the first place in text detection task of the recent ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on Reading Chinese Text on Signboard, further demonstrating its powerful generalization ability. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Detecting text in natural images is challenging when words are small, arbitrarily oriented, elongated, or curved. Existing detectors based on rectangular or quadrilateral regression, including single-shot and direct-regression approaches, offer efficient localization but impose rigid geometric assumptions; segmentation-based and adaptive-boundary methods better accommodate irregular shapes but often require complex proposal grouping or post-processing. This paper proposes TextSnake, a flexible representation and detector for text instances of arbitrary shapes. Rather than describing a word with a fixed bounding box or a variable-length polygon, TextSnake models it as a sequence of overlapping disks whose centers follow the text center line, with each disk characterized by its radius and local orientation. An end-to-end fully convolutional network predicts text regions, center lines, radii, and orientations, from which instances are reconstructed with lightweight geometric processing. The representation naturally covers horizontal, multi-oriented, and curved text while preserving efficiency. Experiments on CTW1500, Total-Text, ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, and MSRA-TD500 demonstrate substantial improvements over contemporary detectors, establishing state-of-the-art performance, particularly for arbitrary-shaped scene text.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation seeks to transfer a classifier trained with labeled source data to an unlabeled target domain, but substantial distribution shifts can make conventional feature alignment unreliable. Existing approaches reduce domain discrepancy through moment matching, kernel-based joint alignment, gradient reversal, or adversarial training; however, global alignment may mix classes, ignore task-specific decision boundaries, and become less effective when several heterogeneous source domains are available. We propose a class-aware adversarial adaptation framework that separates domain-specific variation from transferable semantic features and aligns source and target representations using task-aware discrepancy objectives. Confidence-weighted target pseudo-labels provide class-level guidance, while source-domain weighting prevents a poorly matched source from dominating adaptation. Unlike pixel-level translation and domain-discriminator methods, the proposed approach does not require target annotations or tied source–target encoders, and unlike multi-source moment matching, it explicitly models class structure during alignment. Experiments on standard digit, object-recognition, and multi-source benchmarks show consistent improvements over representative discrepancy-, moment-, and adversarial-based baselines. Ablation studies indicate that semantic alignment and source weighting are complementary, yielding more stable adaptation under large and heterogeneous domain shifts.

original_abstract: The revolution in computer hardware, especially in graphics processing units and tensor processing units, has enabled significant advances in computer graphics and artificial intelligence algorithms. In addition to their many beneficial applications in daily life and business, computer-generated/manipulated images and videos can be used for malicious purposes that violate security systems, privacy, and social trust. The deepfake phenomenon and its variations enable a normal user to use his or her personal computer to easily create fake videos of anybody from a short real online video. Several countermeasures have been introduced to deal with attacks using such videos. However, most of them are targeted at certain domains and are ineffective when applied to other domains or new attacks. In this paper, we introduce a capsule network that can detect various kinds of attacks, from presentation attacks using printed images and replayed videos to attacks using fake videos created using deep learning. It uses many fewer parameters than traditional convolutional neural networks with similar performance. Moreover, we explain, for the first time ever in the literature, the theory behind the application of capsule networks to the forensics problem through detailed analysis and visualization.
generated_abstract: Recent advances in face synthesis, reenactment, swapping, and computer-generated imagery have made forged images and videos increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic media, threatening biometric authentication, digital forensics, and public trust. This paper surveys the development of automated facial-manipulation and presentation-attack detection, tracing the transition from hand-crafted texture and noise descriptors to convolutional, recurrent, capsule, adversarial, and multitask models. It reviews the principal datasets and benchmarks, including FaceForensics and FaceForensics++, and organizes existing methods according to their input modality, learned representations, use of temporal or domain-specific information, and ability to localize tampered regions. In contrast to studies introducing a single detector, the paper proposes a comparative taxonomy and identifies evaluation requirements for robustness to compression, resolution changes, cross-dataset transfer, and previously unseen manipulation techniques. The analysis shows that deep detectors can substantially outperform traditional methods and human observers under matched conditions, but often learn dataset- or manipulation-specific artifacts and degrade under distribution shift. The paper concludes that generalization, explainability, continual adaptation, and realistic large-scale benchmarks remain central challenges for dependable forgery detection.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) produces fluent output but can omit source content, mishandle rare expressions, and fail to reproduce terminology or translations observed in earlier data. Existing remedies either augment attention with retrieved sentence pairs and translation pieces, inject phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT) hypotheses during search, rerank NMT candidates with SMT costs, or combine complete system outputs. These approaches improve adequacy, but typically rely on task-specific heuristics, separate models, or restricted phrase tables. We propose a unified retrieval-guided decoding framework that searches a parallel corpus for source sentences related to the input, extracts aligned target phrases, and integrates their evidence directly into NMT beam search alongside the model’s lexical and contextual probabilities. Retrieved candidates are softly weighted by source similarity, while phrase-level scores and coverage constraints discourage irrelevant or incomplete insertions. The method preserves the fluency and end-to-end training of attention-based NMT while recovering reusable translations without retraining the base system. Experiments across general and narrow-domain language pairs show consistent improvements over strong NMT baselines, especially for rare words, repeated expressions, and domain-specific terminology, with modest computational overhead.

original_abstract: In line with recent advances in neural drug design and sensitivity prediction, we propose a novel architecture for interpretable prediction of anticancer compound sensitivity using a multimodal attention-based convolutional encoder. Our model is based on the three key pillars of drug sensitivity: compounds’ structure in the form of a SMILES sequence, gene expression profiles of tumors and prior knowledge on intracellular interactions from protein-protein interaction networks. We demonstrate that our multiscale convolutional attention-based encoder significantly outperforms a baseline model trained on Morgan fingerprints, a selection of encoders based on SMILES as well as previously reported state of the art for multimodal drug sensitivity prediction (R2 = 0.86 and RMSE = 0.89). Moreover, the explainability of our approach is demonstrated by a thorough analysis of the attention weights. We show that the attended genes significantly enrich apoptotic processes and that the drug attention is strongly correlat...
generated_abstract: Predicting the response of cancer cells or patients to anticancer drugs from molecular profiles is central to precision oncology, yet remains difficult because responses are heterogeneous, measurements are sparse and noisy, and drug and tumor representations are highly dimensional. This paper surveys machine-learning and network-based approaches developed to address this problem, spanning feature-selection and regression models, multitask and ensemble learning, link-prediction and heterogeneous-network formulations, and deep architectures that encode molecular structures, omics profiles, and biological pathways. Building on comparative studies and community benchmarks, it organizes these methods according to their input modalities, learning objectives, response definitions, and validation strategies, rather than introducing another single predictive architecture. It further proposes a practical framework for constructing reproducible drug-response studies, emphasizing leakage-resistant cross-validation, independent datasets, missing-data handling, interpretability, and clinically relevant evaluation. Across the literature, transcriptomic information generally provides the strongest individual signal, while combining complementary molecular and chemical knowledge can improve prediction and biological insight. The review concludes that current performance often overstates translational utility and that robust external validation, mechanistic interpretation, and patient-level data integration are essential for progress toward personalized therapy.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual Question Answering (VQA) systems often achieve high accuracy by exploiting correlations between question wording and answers rather than grounding predictions in image content. This work investigates the language-prior problem and its effect on the reliability and generalization of existing VQA models. Building on balanced datasets such as VQA v2 and changing-prior evaluations such as VQA-CP, as well as adversarial, score-regularization, and unimodal-bias reduction methods, we propose a unified, model-agnostic debiasing framework. The framework trains a question-only bias estimator to identify answer patterns that can be predicted without visual evidence, then uses this signal to reweight learning and encourage predictions whose confidence increases appropriately after incorporating the image. Unlike approaches that modify the dataset or impose strong architectural restrictions, the proposed method can be integrated with diverse multimodal backbones while explicitly measuring residual language bias. Experiments across standard and bias-sensitive VQA benchmarks show that it substantially improves robustness to shifted answer distributions and reduces reliance on unimodal cues, while preserving most of the accuracy obtained on conventional splits. These results demonstrate that effective VQA requires both bias-aware evaluation and visual-grounding-oriented training.

original_abstract: Biological evolution has distilled the experiences of many learners into the general learning algorithms of humans. Our novel meta reinforcement learning algorithm MetaGenRL is inspired by this process. MetaGenRL distills the experiences of many complex agents to meta-learn a low-complexity neural objective function that affects how future individuals will learn. Unlike recent meta-RL algorithms, MetaGenRL can generalize to new environments that are entirely different from those used for meta-training. In some cases, it even outperforms human-engineered RL algorithms. MetaGenRL uses off-policy second-order gradients during meta-training that greatly increase its sample efficiency.
generated_abstract: Reinforcement learning agents remain expensive to train and often require algorithms whose exploration, credit assignment, and update rules are carefully hand-designed. Recent work has begun to address this limitation through meta-learning: recurrent agents can acquire task-specific learning procedures, while learned optimizers, losses, policy gradients, curiosity mechanisms, and adaptive returns can directly automate components of reinforcement learning. This paper reviews and organizes these developments into a unified framework, distinguishing meta-learning representations and initializations from meta-learning the learning algorithm itself. It relates approaches based on slow outer-loop optimization, gradient-based adaptation, recurrent state, program search, and evolutionary or reinforcement-learning-based discovery, highlighting their assumptions, sources of transfer, and modes of generalization. Unlike methods that merely accelerate adaptation by transferring parameters, algorithmic meta-learning seeks procedures that determine how an agent learns and explores. We compare empirical evaluation practices across supervised and reinforcement-learning settings and identify recurring limitations, including costly meta-training, benchmark dependence, instability, and weak out-of-distribution transfer. The review concludes that learned algorithms can match or exceed human-designed baselines, but robust, interpretable, and scalable meta-learning remains an open challenge.

original_abstract: Reed-Muller (RM) codes are among the oldest, simplest and perhaps most ubiquitous family of codes. They are used in many areas of coding theory in both electrical engineering and computer science. Yet, many of their important properties are still under investigation. This paper covers some of the recent developments regarding the weight enumerator and the capacity-achieving properties of RM codes, as well as some of the algorithmic developments. In particular, the paper discusses the recent connections established between RM codes, thresholds of Boolean functions, polarization theory, hypercontractivity, and the techniques of approximating low weight codewords using lower degree polynomials. It then overviews some of the algorithms with performance guarantees, as well as some of the algorithms with state-of-the-art performances in practical regimes. Finally, the paper concludes with a few open problems.
generated_abstract: Reed–Muller (RM) codes combine exceptional symmetry and near-maximum-likelihood performance with a decoding complexity that remains prohibitive at moderate block lengths. Although polar codes provide a capacity-achieving construction from the same Kronecker generator matrix, their channel-dependent bit ordering can perform poorly at finite length, while existing RM decoders based on minimum-weight parity checks or recursive projection and aggregation require substantial computation and offer limited reliability. This paper develops a symmetry-aware recursive decoder for RM codes that combines projection onto lower-order constituent codes with selective aggregation of estimates obtained from code automorphisms. The decoder adapts the set of projections and permutations to the received reliabilities, avoiding the full redundant parity-check or projection collection, and admits parallel implementation. We analyze its complexity and evaluate it on binary erasure, binary symmetric, and additive white Gaussian noise channels over a range of rates and block lengths. The results show substantial gains over conventional successive-cancellation polar decoding and existing low-complexity RM decoders, with performance approaching maximum-likelihood decoding in the short-to-moderate blocklength regime. These findings support RM codes as practical complements to polar codes, not merely asymptotic alternatives.

original_abstract: To ensure pedestrian friendly streets in the era of automated vehicles, reassessment of current policies, practices, design, rules and regulations of urban areas is of importance. This study investigates pedestrian crossing behaviour, as an important element of urban dynamics that is expected to be affected by the presence of automated vehicles. For this purpose, an interpretable machine learning framework is proposed to explore factors affecting pedestrians' wait time before crossing mid-block crosswalks in the presence of automated vehicles. To collect rich behavioural data, we developed a dynamic and immersive virtual reality experiment, with 180 participants from a heterogeneous population in 4 different locations in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). Pedestrian wait time behaviour is then analyzed using a data-driven Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) model, in which the linear combination of the covariates is replaced by a flexible non-linear deep neural network. The proposed model achieved a 5% improvement in goodness of fit, but more importantly, enabled us to incorporate a richer set of covariates. A game theoretic based interpretability method is used to understand the contribution of different covariates to the time pedestrians wait before crossing. Results show that the presence of automated vehicles on roads, wider lane widths, high density on roads, limited sight distance, and lack of walking habits are the main contributing factors to longer wait times. Our study suggested that, to move towards pedestrian-friendly urban areas, national level educational programs for children, enhanced safety measures for seniors, promotion of active modes of transportation, and revised traffic rules and regulations should be considered.
generated_abstract: Autonomous vehicles must anticipate whether pedestrians will cross, yet pedestrian decisions at unsignalized crossings depend on nonlinear interactions among vehicle motion, traffic context, infrastructure, and human perceptions. Existing studies have examined communication cues, trust, external human–machine interfaces, and gap acceptance, but have generally relied on small experiments, conventional statistical models, or prediction-oriented neural networks whose behavioral logic is difficult to inspect. This paper develops an interpretable deep-learning framework for estimating pedestrian crossing decisions and identifying the factors underlying them. Using immersive virtual-reality experiments involving pedestrians interacting with automated and human-driven vehicles, the proposed model learns nonlinear effects and feature interactions while extracting behaviorally meaningful response curves, marginal effects, and individual-level explanations. Its performance and inferred relationships are compared with conventional discrete-choice and artificial-neural-network benchmarks. Results show that the deep model improves predictive accuracy, particularly when crossing behavior varies across traffic and vehicle conditions, while aggregated explanations recover intuitive effects of time to collision, vehicle speed, yielding behavior, crossing type, and pedestrian characteristics. The study also finds that local explanations can be unstable, motivating regularization, model ensembling, and cautious interpretation. The framework offers a practical bridge between flexible prediction and transparent pedestrian-behavior analysis for AV design.

original_abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive ``teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.
generated_abstract: Training deep neural networks remains costly and sensitive to optimization choices, particularly when examples vary substantially in difficulty or contain noise. Existing curriculum-learning methods impose hand-designed orderings, infer difficulty through transfer or learning-progress heuristics, or learn sample selection for a specific student model. This paper proposes an adaptive curriculum framework that jointly exploits the learner’s feedback and the training dynamics of modern architectures. A teacher selects or weights examples, adjusts their difficulty over time, and is optimized to accelerate student improvement rather than merely follow a fixed syllabus. Unlike reverse curricula designed for sparse-reward reinforcement learning and MentorNet-style filtering targeted at corrupted labels, the proposed approach is model- and task-agnostic and can be combined with contemporary optimization practices, including cyclical learning rates. Experiments across recurrent, convolutional, residual, and factorized deep networks, on program execution, speech recognition, and image or text classification, show that adaptive teaching reduces the number of iterations and training examples required to reach a target accuracy. The gains persist across architectures and unfavorable data conditions, while preserving final generalization, demonstrating that learned curricula provide a practical alternative to manual scheduling and uniform sampling.

original_abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks fostered a newfound interest in generative models, resulting in a swelling wave of new works that new-coming researchers may find formidable to surf. In this paper, we intend to help those researchers, by splitting that incoming wave into six "fronts": Architectural Contributions, Conditional Techniques, Normalization and Constraint Contributions, Loss Functions, Image-to-image Translations, and Validation Metrics. The division in fronts organizes literature into approachable blocks, ultimately communicating to the reader how the area is evolving. Previous surveys in the area, which this works also tabulates, focus on a few of those fronts, leaving a gap that we propose to fill with a more integrated, comprehensive overview. Here, instead of an exhaustive survey, we opt for a straightforward review: our target is to be an entry point to this vast literature, and also to be able to update experienced researchers to the newest techniques.
generated_abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have become a central framework for learning complex data distributions, yet their rapid proliferation has produced a fragmented literature and persistent difficulties in training stability, sample diversity, and image fidelity. This paper presents a structured review of GAN research, building on foundational adversarial learning and representative advances in semi-supervised learning, progressive growing, conditional synthesis, Laplacian-pyramid generation, style-based architectures, and large-scale training. Unlike earlier introductions and broad surveys, it organizes developments jointly by architectural design and objective function, relating these choices to the three principal challenges of quality, diversity, and stability. The paper examines major GAN variants, including conditional, Wasserstein, progressive, multi-scale, style-based, and regularized models, and compares their applications in image generation, translation, editing, and representation learning. It also summarizes evaluation measures and discusses limitations such as mode collapse, optimization instability, scalability, and the imperfect correspondence between numerical metrics and human perception. The review concludes that progress has increasingly depended on coordinated architectural and loss innovations, while robust evaluation, controllable diversity, theoretical understanding, and ethically responsible deployment remain open priorities.

original_abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can provide each user with strong privacy guarantees under untrusted data curators while ensuring accurate statistics derived from privatized data. Due to its powerfulness, LDP has been widely adopted to protect privacy in various tasks (e.g., heavy hitters discovery, probability estimation) and systems (e.g., Google Chrome, Apple iOS). Although ${\epsilon}$-LDP has been proposed for many years, the more general notion of $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP has only been studied in very few papers, which mainly consider mean estimation for numeric data. Besides, prior solutions achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP by leveraging Gaussian mechanism, which leads to low accuracy of the aggregated results. In this paper, we propose novel mechanisms that achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP with high utility in data analytics and machine learning. Specifically, we first design $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP algorithms for collecting multi-dimensional numeric data, which can ensure higher accuracy than the optimal Gaussian mechanism while guaranteeing strong privacy for each user. Then, we investigate different local protocols for categorical attributes under $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP. Furthermore, we conduct theoretical analysis on the error bound and variance of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the high data utility of our proposed algorithms on both simple data statistics and complex machine learning models.
generated_abstract: Local differential privacy enables data collection without requiring users to trust an aggregator, but accurate estimation remains difficult for high-dimensional and unbounded data. Existing approaches chiefly address categorical or bounded numerical attributes, often relying on fixed clipping ranges, while theoretical studies of Gaussian estimation establish limits without yielding broadly practical mechanisms. We develop an adaptive local randomization framework for estimating means, distributions, and regression statistics from mixed numerical and categorical records. The method calibrates perturbation to a user’s data and privacy budget, uses robust range adaptation for unbounded observations, and combines unbiased debiasing with an aggregation procedure that supports heterogeneous coordinates. Privacy is proved under both pure and approximate local differential privacy, with Rényi-divergence accounting enabling tighter composition across repeated reports. We derive utility bounds and compare them with minimax lower bounds, showing that the proposed estimators attain near-optimal dependence on sample size, dimension, and privacy. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate substantially lower error than randomized response, generic Gaussian perturbation, and existing multidimensional LDP mechanisms, particularly for heavy-tailed data and downstream linear prediction. These results indicate that adaptive local perturbation can make practical analytics feasible without weakening client-side privacy guarantees.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has achieved strong results with feed-forward agents and distributed experience replay, but many tasks require memory because observations are partial and recurrent agents introduce additional difficulties in off-policy learning. In particular, replayed sequences may be associated with obsolete recurrent states, while recomputing states from sequence boundaries can produce a mismatch between training and acting. We present Recurrent Experience Replay in Distributed Reinforcement Learning (R2D2), a distributed recurrent Q-learning agent that combines prioritized sequence replay with recurrent value estimation. R2D2 addresses state staleness by storing recurrent states with experience and addresses state mismatch through a burn-in period that reconstructs hidden representations before applying learning updates. The architecture builds on distributed prioritized replay and the stabilizing advances of multi-step, distributional, and dueling value methods, while extending them to recurrent agents rather than merely increasing actor throughput. Experiments on the 57 Atari games and DeepMind Lab show that the proposed design substantially improves both data and wall-clock efficiency, achieving state-of-the-art Atari performance and demonstrating that recurrent distributed agents can scale effectively to visually rich, partially observable environments.

original_abstract: The design of deep graph models still remains to be investigated and the crucial part is how to explore and exploit the knowledge from different hops of neighbors in an efficient way. In this paper, we propose a novel RNN-like deep graph neural network architecture by incorporating AdaBoost into the computation of network; and the proposed graph convolutional network called AdaGCN~(AdaBoosting Graph Convolutional Network) has the ability to efficiently extract knowledge from high-order neighbors and integrate knowledge from different hops of neighbors into the network in an AdaBoost way. We also present the architectural difference between AdaGCN and existing graph convolutional methods to show the benefits of our proposal. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art prediction performance and the computational advantage of our approach AdaGCN.
generated_abstract: Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have achieved strong results on graph-structured data, but are typically restricted to shallow architectures: repeated neighborhood aggregation can cause over-smoothing, while limited receptive fields prevent effective modeling of long-range dependencies. Earlier spectral and spatial formulations, including first-order GCNs, attention-based layers, multi-scale filters, and jumping-knowledge schemes, improve propagation or feature selection but do not fully establish how to train very deep graph networks. This paper investigates whether GCNs can be made as deep as convolutional networks on grids. It develops a DeepGCN framework that combines modern deep-network designs—residual and dense skip connections—with graph-specific operations, including dilated neighborhood aggregation, to enlarge receptive fields while preserving discriminative information. The study systematically compares these designs and analyzes their influence on optimization, information flow, and over-smoothing. Experiments on node-classification, graph-classification, and point-cloud tasks show that substantially deeper models can be trained reliably and consistently outperform conventional shallow GCNs and competing graph architectures. The results demonstrate that depth is not intrinsically incompatible with graph convolution; appropriate connectivity and dilation can unlock more expressive, scalable graph representations.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: Massive MIMO combines the spatial multiplexing capability of large antenna arrays with NOMA’s ability to serve users on shared time-frequency resources, but their interaction is not straightforward. Favorable propagation and channel hardening can make inter-user interference negligible, whereas correlated or non-hardening channels may invalidate conventional rate analyses and decoding assumptions. This paper develops an analytical framework for downlink massive-MIMO NOMA that accounts for imperfect CSI, user grouping, successive interference cancellation, and finite coherence blocks. Building on existing massive-MIMO and multiple-antenna NOMA designs, it departs from idealized orthogonality, perfect user ordering, and asymptotic channel hardening by evaluating both hardening and non-hardening propagation with ergodic-rate bounds that remain useful when effective beamformed gains fluctuate. A low-complexity grouping and power-allocation strategy is proposed, pairing users with sufficiently distinct effective gains while exploiting spatial separation to reduce SIC overhead and feedback requirements. Analysis and simulations show that NOMA provides meaningful gains mainly in overloaded, correlated, or CSI-limited channels. When propagation is favorable and many antennas efficiently separate users, conventional multiuser beamforming is generally superior, identifying the operating regimes in which NOMA is justified for massive-MIMO networks.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: Few-shot learning seeks to enable models to recognize or solve novel tasks from only a handful of labeled examples, overcoming the data requirements and slow adaptation of conventional supervised deep learning. Building on metric-based approaches such as Matching, Prototypical, and Relation Networks, optimization-based methods including MAML and its stabilized variants, and generative, probabilistic, transfer, and hierarchical meta-learning, this paper organizes the rapidly expanding literature around how prior experience is represented and how adaptation is performed. Rather than introducing another task-specific learner, it provides a unified taxonomy and critically compares the assumptions, training procedures, and evaluation settings underlying existing methods. The review also considers extensions to zero-shot learning, regression, reinforcement learning, heterogeneous tasks, and synthetic example generation, highlighting the effects of episode construction, architecture, and data distribution on reported performance. Across benchmarks, meta-learned representations and carefully designed inductive biases substantially improve adaptation in genuinely low-data regimes, but gains are sensitive to task similarity and evaluation protocol. The paper concludes that robust generalization beyond the training-task distribution, uncertainty estimation, computational efficiency, and standardized experiments remain central open challenges.

original_abstract: Edge computing is an emerging concept based on distributing computing, storage, and control services closer to end network nodes. Edge computing lies at the heart of the fifth generation (5G) wireless systems and beyond. While current state-of-the-art networks communicate, compute, and process data in a centralized manner (at the cloud), for latency and compute-centric applications, both radio access and computational resources must be brought closer to the edge, harnessing the availability of computing and storage-enabled small cell base stations in proximity to the end devices. Furthermore, the network infrastructure must enable a distributed edge decision-making service that learns to adapt to the network dynamics with minimal latency and optimize network deployment and operation accordingly. This article will provide a fresh look to the concept of edge computing by first discussing the applications that the network edge must provide, with a special emphasis on the ensuing challenges in enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency edge computing services for mission-critical applications such as virtual reality (VR), vehicle-to-everything (V2X), edge artificial intelligence (AI), and so forth. Furthermore, several case studies where the edge is key are explored followed by insights and prospect for future work.
generated_abstract: Ultra-reliable and low-latency applications in 5G and beyond require mobile edge computing systems to account for rare queueing and communication failures rather than optimize average delay or throughput. Existing studies impose probabilistic queue constraints and use extreme-value theory, Lyapunov optimization, and matching-based association to manage offloading and resources; however, they largely treat mobility, wireless connectivity, computation, and reliability in isolation. This paper develops a unified framework for mobility-aware, risk-sensitive task offloading in heterogeneous edge networks. It jointly determines user–server association, local execution, transmission power, and computational resources over two timescales, while incorporating channel intermittency, handover costs, server workload, and tail latency constraints. Unlike conventional received-power handover and average-based MEC designs, the proposed policy uses reliability-aware association and dynamic short-term control to preserve service continuity under rapidly varying conditions, including mmWave blockage and spatio-temporal user mobility. Lyapunov drift-plus-penalty methods provide online decisions, while statistical tail constraints capture rare queue violations. Numerical experiments show that the framework substantially improves reliability and latency and reduces device energy consumption relative to fixed-association, average-delay, and conventional handover baselines, at a manageable computational cost.

original_abstract: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) aims to correct systematic errors in a machine translated text. This is primarily useful when the machine translation (MT) system is not accessible for improvement, leaving APE as a viable option to improve translation quality as a downstream task - which is the focus of this thesis. This field has received less attention compared to MT due to several reasons, which include: the limited availability of data to perform a sound research, contrasting views reported by different researchers about the effectiveness of APE, and limited attention from the industry to use APE in current production pipelines. In this thesis, we perform a thorough investigation of APE as a downstream task in order to: i) understand its potential to improve translation quality; ii) advance the core technology - starting from classical methods to recent deep-learning based solutions; iii) cope with limited and sparse data; iv) better leverage multiple input sources; v) mitigate the task-specific problem of over-correction; vi) enhance neural decoding to leverage external knowledge; and vii) establish an online learning framework to handle data diversity in real-time. All the above contributions are discussed across several chapters, and most of them are evaluated in the APE shared task organized each year at the Conference on Machine Translation. Our efforts in improving the technology resulted in the best system at the 2017 APE shared task, and our work on online learning received a distinguished paper award at the Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics. Overall, outcomes and findings of our work have boost interest among researchers and attracted industries to examine this technology to solve real-word problems.
generated_abstract: Automatic post-editing (APE) seeks to improve machine-translated text without modifying or accessing the internal decoder of the underlying translation system, thereby reducing human post-editing effort. This paper surveys the development of APE from rule-based and statistical approaches to recent neural systems. It reviews methods that model the task as monolingual correction, bilingual translation, or multi-source generation from the source sentence and the machine-translation hypothesis, and examines advances including attention, factored inputs, ensembles, reranking, synthetic training data, online adaptation, and quality-estimation-informed selection. In contrast to earlier studies that report isolated shared-task systems or compare only a small set of methods, the paper organizes the literature around architectures, supervision, data requirements, evaluation procedures, and practical constraints. It also discusses the relationship between APE and related tasks such as quality estimation and translation correction, highlighting the risks of overcorrection and inadequate training data. The analysis concludes that neural multi-source models generally provide the strongest and most portable improvements, although gains depend substantially on initial translation quality and domain. It identifies reproducibility, realistic evaluation, limited data, and faithful minimal editing as persistent challenges.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: Online decision problems must balance the robustness of worst-case algorithms with the potential benefits of data-driven predictions. Existing work has incorporated machine-learned advice into caching, ski rental, scheduling, and advertising, but typically assumes that prediction quality is summarized by an abstract error measure or studies only worst-case guarantees. This paper develops a learning-augmented approach to ski rental that uses a prediction of the customer’s rental horizon while remaining effective when that prediction is inaccurate. Building on prediction-enhanced online algorithms, it introduces a conservative buying strategy that interpolates between the prediction-driven decision and the classical rent-then-buy rule, and analyzes its performance through both consistency and robustness. In contrast to average-case analyses based on a specified distribution of rental durations, the proposed method does not require a probabilistic model and provides guarantees for every input sequence, parameterized by prediction error. The analysis shows that accurate forecasts yield substantially lower cost than the traditional worst-case strategy, while adversarial or highly inaccurate forecasts cause only bounded degradation. Thus, machine-learned predictions can improve ski-rental decisions without sacrificing the fundamental protection of online algorithms.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to automate networking tasks, including routing, packet classification, query optimization, traffic modeling, and adaptive video delivery. Although these systems can outperform handcrafted techniques, their black-box decisions make it difficult to assess reliability, diagnose failures, and establish correctness or security. This paper surveys interpretability and verification techniques relevant to machine-learning-driven networked systems. It organizes existing work along complementary dimensions: intrinsic versus post-hoc explanations, global versus local analysis, feature- and structure-based explanations, and empirical versus formal guarantees. Building on general approaches such as Network Dissection, SHAP, and GNNExplainer, the survey examines how these ideas apply to neural and reinforcement-learning systems operating on sequential, structured, and graph-based network data. It also contrasts explanation with verification, emphasizing that intuitive feature attributions do not necessarily establish behavioral safety. Through a review of representative networking systems and evaluation practices, the paper identifies limitations in current benchmarks, explanation fidelity, generalization beyond observed conditions, and human-centered evaluation. It concludes with open challenges and design principles for developing network automation that is not only performant, but interpretable, trustworthy, and verifiable.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: Reinforcement learning offers effective control in complex environments, but its trial-and-error exploration can violate safety requirements, particularly when system dynamics and performance objectives are unknown. This paper reviews and organizes recent approaches that combine reinforcement learning with formal specifications, focusing on temporal-logic constraints for Markov decision processes. It contrasts model-based PAC learning and product-MDP methods with model-free, automata-guided reward shaping, and examines safety-constrained exploration, shields, permissive strategies, adaptive padding, and verification-preserving model updates. Unlike prior contributions that introduce or evaluate a single synthesis procedure, the paper develops a unified taxonomy along three dimensions: the information available about the environment, the mechanism enforcing logical constraints, and the strength and type of resulting guarantees. It further compares methods according to correctness, optimality, convergence, scalability, and their ability to operate under model uncertainty or heterogeneous environments. The analysis shows that formal constraints can substantially improve safety and exploration efficiency, but often introduce computational or conservatism tradeoffs; asymptotic optimality and strict safety are rarely obtained simultaneously in fully unknown settings. The paper concludes with design guidelines and open challenges for scalable, verifiable safe reinforcement learning.

original_abstract: Many inferential and learning tasks can be accomplished efficiently by means of distributed optimization algorithms where the network topology plays a critical role in driving the local interactions among neighboring agents. There is a large body of literature examining the effect of the graph structure on the performance of optimization strategies. In this article, we examine the inverse problem and consider the reverse question: How much information does observing the behavior at the nodes convey about the underlying network structure used for optimization? Over large-scale networks, the difficulty of addressing such inverse questions (or problems) is compounded by the fact that usually only a limited portion of nodes can be probed, giving rise to a second important question: Despite the presence of several unobserved nodes, are partial and local observations still sufficient to discover the graph linking the probed nodes? The article surveys recent advances on this inverse learning problem and related questions. Examples of applications are provided to illustrate how the interplay between graph learning and distributed optimization arises in practice, e.g., in cognitive engineered systems such as distributed detection, or in other real-world problems such as the mechanism of opinion formation over social networks and the mechanism of coordination in biological networks. A unifying framework for examining the reconstruction error will be described, which allows to devise and examine various estimation strategies enabling successful graph learning. The relevance of specific network attributes, such as sparsity versus density of connections, and node degree concentration, is discussed in relation to the topology inference goal. It is shown how universal (i.e., data-driven) clustering algorithms can be exploited to solve the graph learning problem.
generated_abstract: Inferring network structure from dynamical data is especially challenging when observations are indirect and available only from a small subset of agents. This paper studies local tomography over diffusion and adaptive networks, seeking to recover the interaction subgraph among observable agents while treating the remaining network as latent. Building on graph-signal-processing approaches based on covariance and spectral structure, and on recent tomography results for Erdős–Rényi latent graphs, we depart from assumptions of full observability and sparse connectivity. We develop and analyze estimators of the agents’ combination matrix, including lagged correlation, residual, and Granger-type constructions, and combine them with universal clustering to distinguish interacting from non-interacting pairs. The analysis identifies concentration of latent node degrees—and the resulting asymptotic separation of estimator entries—as the key source of identifiability, rather than sparsity itself. We establish conditions under which the observable subgraph is recovered consistently, including dense regimes and, where applicable, asymmetric adaptive policies, and characterize the effect of network size, observation fraction, and time horizon. Simulations support the theory and show that simple estimators can outperform full-observability-optimal methods under partial observation.

original_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently led to many breakthroughs on a range of complex control tasks. However, the agent's decision-making process is generally not transparent. The lack of interpretability hinders the applicability of RL in safety-critical scenarios. While several methods have attempted to interpret vision-based RL, most come without detailed explanation for the agent's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised interpretable framework, which can discover causal features to enable easy interpretation of RL agents even for non-experts. Specifically, a self-supervised interpretable network (SSINet) is employed to produce fine-grained attention masks for highlighting task-relevant information, which constitutes most evidence for the agent's decisions. We verify and evaluate our method on several Atari 2600 games as well as Duckietown, which is a challenging self-driving car simulator environment. The results show that our method renders causal explanations and empirical evidences about how the agent makes decisions and why the agent performs well or badly, especially when transferred to novel scenes. Overall, our method provides valuable insight into the internal decision-making process of vision-based RL. In addition, our method does not use any external labelled data, and thus demonstrates the possibility to learn high-quality mask through a self-supervised manner, which may shed light on new paradigms for label-free vision learning such as self-supervised segmentation and detection.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning agents can achieve outstanding performance while offering little insight into the visual evidence and strategies underlying their decisions. Existing work has explored attention-augmented Q-networks, saliency maps, perturbation-based explanations, interpretable architectures, and self-supervised attention, but these approaches differ substantially in whether they improve learning, faithfully represent the policy, or merely provide plausible visualizations. This paper reviews and organizes research on interpreting vision-based reinforcement-learning agents, with particular emphasis on Atari environments. It develops a taxonomy spanning intrinsic interpretability, post-hoc saliency, attention mechanisms, feature and policy analysis, and human-centered evaluation, and contrasts their assumptions, computational costs, and validation procedures. Building on prior demonstrations that attention can expose spatial and temporal decision cues, the paper argues that attention alone is not sufficient evidence of causal importance; explanations should be tested through perturbation, counterfactual analysis, generalization, and behavioral agreement. The review identifies recurring limitations, including shallow or overfit representations, weak faithfulness metrics, and reliance on game-specific benchmarks, and proposes directions for standardized evaluation and more reliable, actionable explanations for deep reinforcement-learning policies.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: Automatic testing of heap-manipulating programs remains difficult: symbolic execution captures structural path constraints but suffers from path explosion and may produce infeasible or unusable heaps, whereas search-based testing can construct legal inputs but often misses paths whose reachability depends on complex data-structure shape. This paper presents a hybrid, compositional approach that combines separation-logic symbolic execution with search-guided input construction. Symbolic execution derives shape, size, and value constraints, using user-defined heap predicates and bag properties to describe both structure and contents; a search procedure then synthesizes sequences of interface operations that instantiate valid inputs satisfying selected constraints. Unlike whole-program symbolic testing and bi-abductive compositional analyses, the method delegates difficult constraint solving and input construction to directed search, while retaining symbolic reasoning for path selection. It also improves on prior hybrid fuzzing and concolic techniques by operating over structured heaps rather than primarily byte-level inputs, and by rejecting partially initialized states. An implementation is evaluated on programs and data-structure libraries with complex heap inputs. The results indicate improved coverage, fewer invalid test cases, and greater scalability than symbolic or search-based testing alone.

original_abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation usually assumes that the controlled attribute can take on one of a small set of values known a priori. In this work, we propose a novel task, where the syntax of a generated sentence is controlled rather by a sentential exemplar. To evaluate quantitatively with standard metrics, we create a novel dataset with human annotations. We also develop a variational model with a neural module specifically designed for capturing syntactic knowledge and several multitask training objectives to promote disentangled representation learning. Empirically, the proposed model is observed to achieve improvements over baselines and learn to capture desirable characteristics.
generated_abstract: Neural text generators produce fluent outputs, but often lack global structure, controllability, and diversity, while latent-variable models are difficult to train and retrieval-based systems may copy their exemplars. This paper investigates whether generation can be improved by combining continuous sentence representations with explicit, reusable generation plans. Building on variational autoencoders for holistic sentence modeling, disentangled representations for separating semantic factors, and prototype- and exemplar-based decoders for exploiting observed language patterns, we propose a retrieval-guided latent generation framework. The model first identifies a relevant prototype or soft template, encodes the desired content and stylistic properties, and then performs neural editing conditioned on both the retrieved structure and continuous latent variables. Auxiliary reconstruction, attribute, and content-preservation objectives encourage interpretable controls while reducing posterior collapse and unnecessary copying. Experiments on language generation and controlled rewriting tasks show that the proposed approach generates more fluent, diverse, and coherent sentences than left-to-right, standard VAE, and purely retrieval-based baselines. Qualitative analyses further reveal meaningful latent edits and improved control over sentence-level attributes, demonstrating that retrieval and neural generation are complementary rather than competing paradigms.

original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) provide rich spectral information that contributed to the successful performance improvement of numerous computer vision tasks. However, it can only be achieved at the expense of images' spatial resolution. Hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) addresses this problem by fusing low resolution (LR) HSI with multispectral image (MSI) carrying much higher spatial resolution (HR). All existing HSI-SR approaches require the LR HSI and HR MSI to be well registered and the reconstruction accuracy of the HR HSI relies heavily on the registration accuracy of different modalities. This paper exploits the uncharted problem domain of HSI-SR without the requirement of multi-modality registration. Given the unregistered LR HSI and HR MSI with overlapped regions, we design a unique unsupervised learning structure linking the two unregistered modalities by projecting them into the same statistical space through the same encoder. The mutual information (MI) is further adopted to capture the non-linear statistical dependencies between the representations from two modalities (carrying spatial information) and their raw inputs. By maximizing the MI, spatial correlations between different modalities can be well characterized to further reduce the spectral distortion. A collaborative $l_{2,1}$ norm is employed as the reconstruction error instead of the more common $l_2$ norm, so that individual pixels can be recovered as accurately as possible. With this design, the network allows to extract correlated spectral and spatial information from unregistered images that better preserves the spectral information. The proposed method is referred to as unregistered and unsupervised mutual Dirichlet Net ($u^2$-MDN). Extensive experimental results using benchmark HSI datasets demonstrate the superior performance of $u^2$-MDN as compared to the state-of-the-art.
generated_abstract: High-resolution hyperspectral imagery is valuable for material identification and scene analysis, yet current sensors commonly trade spatial resolution for spectral fidelity. Existing hyperspectral super-resolution methods address this problem through handcrafted low-rank or tensor priors, supervised convolutional networks, or unsupervised coupled autoencoders. Their effectiveness is limited by the need for representative high-resolution training data, inaccurate assumptions about point-spread and spectral-response functions, and inadequate control of spectral distortion. We propose an unsupervised, model-guided deep fusion framework that reconstructs a high-resolution hyperspectral image from a low-resolution hyperspectral image and a high-resolution multispectral observation. The network combines spatial–spectral residual learning with an explicit observation model, while jointly estimating the latent image and the sensor degradation operators. Physics-consistent reconstruction losses, spectral-angle regularization, and cross-modal feature coupling provide self-supervision without requiring ground-truth high-resolution hyperspectral data. Unlike purely data-driven CNNs, the proposed architecture preserves measurement fidelity; unlike conventional optimization and tensor methods, it learns adaptable nonlinear priors end to end. Experiments on simulated and real datasets demonstrate improved spatial detail, spectral fidelity, robustness to unknown sensor responses, and competitive computational efficiency over representative state-of-the-art methods.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: We study unsupervised visual representation learning, where the absence of manual labels must be overcome without sacrificing the quality and transferability of learned features. Building on instance-discrimination, predictive coding, and mutual-information approaches, we introduce SimCLR, a simple contrastive framework that learns by maximizing agreement between two independently augmented views of the same image while contrasting them with views from other images. Unlike earlier methods that rely on specialized pretext tasks, memory banks, or complex architectures, SimCLR uses standard neural networks and derives its effectiveness from a carefully designed composition of augmentations, a learnable nonlinear projection head, and a normalized temperature-scaled contrastive objective. Extensive experiments show that augmentation composition is crucial, and that projecting representations before applying the contrastive loss substantially improves downstream performance. With sufficiently large batches and longer training, SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet under linear evaluation, improving substantially over previous self-supervised methods and narrowing the gap with supervised pretraining. Its representations also transfer competitively to object detection and other classification tasks, demonstrating that a comparatively simple contrastive recipe can provide broadly useful visual features.

original_abstract: Existing analysis work in machine reading comprehension (MRC) is largely concerned with evaluating the capabilities of systems. However, the capabilities of datasets are not assessed for benchmarking language understanding precisely. We propose a semi-automated, ablation-based methodology for this challenge; By checking whether questions can be solved even after removing features associated with a skill requisite for language understanding, we evaluate to what degree the questions do not require the skill. Experiments on 10 datasets (e.g., CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) with a strong baseline model show that, for example, the relative scores of a baseline model provided with content words only and with shuffled sentence words in the context are on average 89.2% and 78.5% of the original score, respectively. These results suggest that most of the questions already answered correctly by the model do not necessarily require grammatical and complex reasoning. For precise benchmarking, MRC datasets will need to take extra care in their design to ensure that questions can correctly evaluate the intended skills.
generated_abstract: We present DROP, a crowdsourced reading-comprehension benchmark designed to evaluate discrete reasoning over paragraphs. Existing datasets such as SQuAD and its adversarial and unanswerable extensions have driven substantial progress, but many questions can be answered through lexical matching or extraction of a contiguous text span. Although newer resources target conversational context, paraphrase, or multi-sentence inference, they seldom require models to manipulate information explicitly. DROP addresses this gap with questions whose answers require reading a passage and performing operations such as addition, subtraction, comparison, counting, or sorting over entities and quantities mentioned in it. The dataset contains approximately 96,000 questions associated with more than 6,000 passages drawn from diverse domains; answers may be spans, numbers, or lists. We evaluate strong neural reading-comprehension baselines and show that they perform substantially below humans, despite achieving near-human results on conventional benchmarks. These findings indicate that current systems often exploit surface cues rather than robust comprehension and motivate models that combine language understanding with explicit, compositional numerical reasoning.

original_abstract: Spatio-temporal action localization is a challenging yet fascinating task that aims to detect and classify human actions in video clips. In this paper, we develop a high-level video understanding module which can encode interactions between actors and objects both in space and time. In our formulation, spatio-temporal relationships are learned by performing self-attention operations on a graph structure connecting entities from consecutive clips. Noticeably, the use of graph learning is unprecedented for this task. From a computational point of view, the proposed module is backbone independent by design and does not need end-to-end training. When tested on the AVA dataset, it demonstrates a 10-16% relative mAP improvement over the baseline. Further, it can outperform or bring performances comparable to state-of-the-art models which require heavy end-to-end and synchronized training on multiple GPUs. Code is publicly available at: this https URL.
generated_abstract: We address the challenge of learning discriminative representations for human actions that unfold over long and varied temporal intervals. Existing two-stream models separate appearance and motion, while 3D and factorized spatiotemporal convolutions learn joint representations but often rely on fixed temporal resolutions and expensive processing. We propose a unified multiscale spatiotemporal network that combines a high-resolution motion pathway with a low-resolution semantic pathway. Factorized three-dimensional residual blocks are used to encode appearance and motion efficiently, and lateral connections progressively fuse information across temporal scales. Unlike methods that classify independently sampled snippets or generate and associate action proposals in separate stages, our framework learns recognition and localization features end to end and preserves temporal continuity through a tube-aware prediction head. Experiments on standard action-recognition and action-detection benchmarks show that multiscale temporal processing and cross-pathway fusion consistently improve over conventional two-stream, C3D, R(2+1)D, and SlowFast-style baselines. The results demonstrate that efficient joint modeling of semantics, fine-grained motion, and long-range temporal structure provides a robust basis for both classifying actions and localizing them in untrimmed video.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks.
