Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks deliver high accuracy at the cost of substantial memory, computation, and energy, limiting their deployment on mobile and embedded hardware. Prior work has shown that binary or ternary weights, low-bit activations, and integer-valued training can replace multiplications with bit operations, but fixed quantization rules and separately designed parameterizations often produce significant accuracy loss or restrict the applicable bitwidths. This paper develops a learned, task-aware quantization framework in which the network’s weights and activations are represented with low-bit integers while the quantization step sizes are optimized jointly with the model parameters. Straight-through gradient estimation enables end-to-end training despite the discrete forward computation, and the resulting operators remain compatible with efficient fixed-point and bitwise hardware. Unlike BinaryConnect, ternary-weight methods, and stochastic low-precision training schemes, the approach does not rely on manually selected thresholds or a single prescribed precision; it adapts quantization scales to each layer and supports arbitrary bitwidths. Experiments across common convolutional architectures and CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate accuracy close to, and in several settings matching or exceeding, full-precision and previous quantized baselines, while substantially reducing model size and computational cost.

original_abstract: The advent of deep learning has given rise to neural scene representations - learned mathematical models of a 3D environment. However, many of these representations do not explicitly reason about geometry and thus do not account for the underlying 3D structure of the scene. In contrast, geometric deep learning has explored 3D-structure-aware representations of scene geometry, but requires explicit 3D supervision. We propose Scene Representation Networks (SRNs), a continuous, 3D-structure-aware scene representation that encodes both geometry and appearance. SRNs represent scenes as continuous functions that map world coordinates to a feature representation of local scene properties. By formulating the image formation as a differentiable ray-marching algorithm, SRNs can be trained end-to-end from only 2D observations, without access to depth or geometry. This formulation naturally generalizes across scenes, learning powerful geometry and appearance priors in the process. We demonstrate the potential of SRNs by evaluating them for novel view synthesis, few-shot reconstruction, joint shape and appearance interpolation, and unsupervised discovery of a non-rigid face model.
generated_abstract: Recovering complete 3D object geometry from a single image remains difficult because the observation is ambiguous, occluded, and lacks reliable depth. Existing learning-based methods address this problem with voxel grids, point clouds, parametric patches, or implicit functions, while view-synthesis and generative models exploit multi-view consistency but often do not produce an explicit, high-quality surface. We propose a single-image reconstruction framework that combines a convolutional image encoder with a continuous 3D representation and differentiable projection. The model predicts geometry in function space rather than a fixed-resolution voxel grid, and is trained using rendered silhouettes, depth, and image-consistency losses, thereby reducing its dependence on dense 3D supervision. Unlike prior approaches that separately infer views or sacrifice efficiency for resolution, our method directly recovers detailed surfaces at arbitrary resolution and can incorporate multiple observations when available. Experiments on synthetic object benchmarks and challenging real images show improved geometric accuracy, completeness, and visual fidelity over voxel-, point-, and view-based baselines. The results demonstrate that differentiable image formation and continuous shape representations provide a practical route to robust, scalable single-view 3D reconstruction.

original_abstract: AI Ethics is now a global topic of discussion in academic and policy circles. At least 84 public-private initiatives have produced statements describing high-level principles, values, and other tenets to guide the ethical development, deployment, and governance of AI. According to recent meta-analyses, AI Ethics has seemingly converged on a set of principles that closely resemble the four classic principles of medical ethics. Despite the initial credibility granted to a principled approach to AI Ethics by the connection to principles in medical ethics, there are reasons to be concerned about its future impact on AI development and governance. Significant differences exist between medicine and AI development that suggest a principled approach in the latter may not enjoy success comparable to the former. Compared to medicine, AI development lacks (1) common aims and fiduciary duties, (2) professional history and norms, (3) proven methods to translate principles into practice, and (4) robust legal and professional accountability mechanisms. These differences suggest we should not yet celebrate consensus around high-level principles that hide deep political and normative disagreement.
generated_abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed in decisions that shape access to opportunities, services, and rights, yet existing approaches to AI ethics remain divided between high-level principles and narrowly targeted technical interventions. This paper examines how ethical commitments can be made actionable across the AI lifecycle. Building on analyses of ethics guidelines, algorithmic opacity, fairness tools, moral preferences, and professional codes, it moves beyond cataloguing principles or treating compliance as a sufficient safeguard. Through a critical synthesis of the literature, it identifies recurrent gaps between stated values and organizational practice, including ambiguous concepts, unclear responsibility, limited stakeholder participation, and weak mechanisms for monitoring and redress. The paper proposes a socio-technical framework for responsible AI that links ethical principles to context-sensitive impact assessment, participatory requirements, documentation, design and evaluation practices, deployment governance, and ongoing audit. It further distinguishes measures that can be supported by technical tools from those requiring institutional or legal intervention. The analysis concludes that ethical AI cannot be achieved through guidelines or codes alone; it requires explicit accountability, interdisciplinary collaboration, and governance embedded throughout system development and use.

original_abstract: This paper develops several average-case reduction techniques to show new hardness results for three central high-dimensional statistics problems, implying a statistical-computational gap induced by robustness, a detection-recovery gap and a universality principle for these gaps. A main feature of our approach is to map to these problems via a common intermediate problem that we introduce, which we call Imbalanced Sparse Gaussian Mixtures. We assume the planted clique conjecture for a version of the planted clique problem where the position of the planted clique is mildly constrained, and from this obtain the following computational lower bounds: (1) a $k$-to-$k^2$ statistical-computational gap for robust sparse mean estimation, providing the first average-case evidence for a conjecture of Li (2017) and Balakrishnan et al. (2017); (2) a tight lower bound for semirandom planted dense subgraph, which shows that a semirandom adversary shifts the detection threshold in planted dense subgraph to the conjectured recovery threshold; and (3) a universality principle for $k$-to-$k^2$ gaps in a broad class of sparse mixture problems that includes many natural formulations such as the spiked covariance model. #R##N#Our main approach is to introduce several average-case techniques to produce structured and Gaussianized versions of an input graph problem, and then to rotate these high-dimensional Gaussians by matrices carefully constructed from hyperplanes in $\mathbb{F}_r^t$. For our universality result, we introduce a new method to perform an algorithmic change of measure tailored to sparse mixtures. We also provide evidence that the mild promise in our variant of planted clique does not change the complexity of the problem.
generated_abstract: High-dimensional inference problems often admit statistically optimal procedures that are computationally infeasible, while efficient algorithms require substantially stronger signals. This paper surveys and organizes the emerging theory of such statistical–computational tradeoffs across planted clustering, submatrix detection and localization, sparse PCA, sparse matrix detection, and related models. Building on reconstruction thresholds and minimax limits, it contrasts information-theoretic impossibility with algorithmic barriers established through planted-clique reductions, statistical-query lower bounds, and discretization or average-case reduction techniques. It also relates convex relaxations, spectral and local methods, exhaustive search, and semidefinite programming to the distinct regimes in which they succeed, and discusses robustness under semirandom perturbations. Unlike work focused on a single model or a single hardness conjecture, the paper emphasizes common mechanisms, universality, and the dependence of computational thresholds on signal distributions, sparsity, and loss functions. It proposes a unified taxonomy separating impossible, statistically feasible but computationally hard, efficiently solvable, and simple regimes, while identifying limitations of current lower-bound methods and assumptions. The paper concludes that gaps between statistical and computational optimality are widespread and structurally meaningful, motivating robust reductions and new algorithms that narrow them.

original_abstract: The desire to map neural networks to varying-capacity devices has led to the development of a wealth of compression techniques, many of which involve replacing standard convolutional blocks in a large network with cheap alternative blocks. However, not all blocks are created equally; for a required compute budget there may exist a potent combination of many different cheap blocks, though exhaustively searching for such a combination is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we develop BlockSwap: a fast algorithm for choosing networks with interleaved block types by passing a single minibatch of training data through randomly initialised networks and gauging their Fisher potential. These networks can then be used as students and distilled with the original large network as a teacher. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the chosen networks across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet for classification, and COCO for detection, and provide a comprehensive ablation study of our approach. BlockSwap quickly explores possible block configurations using a simple architecture ranking system, yielding highly competitive networks in orders of magnitude less time than most architecture search techniques (e.g. under 5 minutes on a single GPU for CIFAR-10). Code is available at https://github.com/BayesWatch/pytorch-blockswap.
generated_abstract: Training large neural networks is expensive because both optimization and inference involve far more parameters than are apparently necessary. Existing compression methods typically prune a pretrained dense model, while sparse-from-scratch approaches often fix a random connectivity pattern or rely on heuristics that are unrelated to the task. We propose a dynamic sparse training method that maintains a fixed parameter budget throughout optimization. At regular intervals, connections with the smallest magnitudes are removed and an equal number of new connections are created at locations with the largest gradient-based importance. This procedure combines the task awareness of sensitivity-based pruning with the flexibility of continual rewiring, while avoiding the storage and optimization cost of a dense, permanently trained model. Unlike neuron pruning, learned filter groups, and architecture search, our method preserves the original network’s computational structure and can be applied to convolutional and residual architectures without redesign. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks, including CIFAR and ImageNet, show that dynamically rewired sparse networks can match or closely approach dense-network accuracy across several architectures, substantially reducing parameter storage and training cost.

original_abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of generating a set ofrealistic and diverse backgrounds when given only a smallforeground region. We refer to this task as image outpaint-ing. The technical challenge of this task is to synthesize notonly plausible but also diverse image outputs. Traditionalgenerative adversarial networks suffer from mode collapse.While recent approaches propose to maximize orpreserve the pairwise distance between generated sampleswith respect to their latent distance, they do not explicitlyprevent the diverse samples of different conditional inputsfrom collapsing. Therefore, we propose a new regulariza-tion method to encourage diverse sampling in conditionalsynthesis. In addition, we propose a feature pyramid dis-criminator to improve the image quality. Our experimen-tal results show that our model can produce more diverseimages without sacrificing visual quality compared to state-of-the-arts approaches in both the CelebA face dataset and the Cityscape scene dataset.
generated_abstract: Generating realistic images containing specified objects, appearances, and spatial relationships remains difficult because holistic generative models often lose object identity, while direct compositing produces incompatible scale, pose, lighting, and context. Building on scene-graph generation, text-to-image synthesis, contextual object placement, and GAN-based image editing, we propose an object-centric framework for controllable scene synthesis. The method represents a target scene through object instances and their relations, retrieves or encodes appearance cues from reference images, predicts a coherent layout, and uses a context-aware generator to harmonize inserted objects with the surrounding scene. Adversarial and perceptual objectives encourage both global realism and local fidelity, while a diversity constraint enables multiple plausible realizations of the same specification. Unlike prior inpainting and image-compositing methods, our approach does not merely fill a fixed hole or geometrically warp a foreground; it jointly models where objects should occur and how they should appear in context. Experiments on challenging natural-image datasets show improved realism, object-level consistency, and placement accuracy over existing synthesis and compositing baselines. The results demonstrate that explicit object and relationship modeling provides an effective basis for controllable, diverse image generation and data augmentation.

original_abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) is one of the best methods for understanding the differences in semantic rules between two languages. Especially for Indo-European languages, subword-level models have achieved impressive results. However, when the translation task involves Chinese, semantic granularity remains at the word and character level, so there is still need more fine-grained translation model of Chinese. In this paper, we introduce a simple and effective method for Chinese translation at the sub-character level. Our approach uses the Wubi method to translate Chinese into English; byte-pair encoding (BPE) is then applied. Our method for Chinese-English translation eliminates the need for a complicated word segmentation algorithm during preprocessing. Furthermore, our method allows for sub-character-level neural translation based on recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture, without preprocessing. The empirical results show that for Chinese-English translation tasks, our sub-character-level model has a comparable BLEU score to the subword model, despite having a much smaller vocabulary. Additionally, the small vocabulary is highly advantageous for NMT model compression.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation has traditionally relied on word-based vocabularies, which limit coverage of rare and unseen forms and are particularly problematic for morphologically rich languages and languages with distinct writing systems. Recent character-, subword-, and hybrid word–character models alleviate these limitations, but their relative advantages in accuracy, efficiency, and representation remain unclear. This paper systematically investigates open-vocabulary neural translation by comparing word, subword, character, and hybrid architectures within an attention-based encoder–decoder framework. Building on alignment-based NMT and byte-pair encoding, it evaluates whether explicit segmentation is necessary and whether character information is most effective in the encoder, decoder, or both. The study further examines convolutional composition, multilingual sharing, and reversible decomposition of Chinese characters through ASCII-based encodings. Across multiple WMT language pairs, including morphologically rich and typologically diverse settings, character-aware models substantially reduce unknown-word errors and improve translation of inflections, names, compounds, and novel forms. However, fully character-level systems incur considerable computational costs and may struggle across writing systems, whereas subword and hybrid models provide a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off. The results support adaptive open-vocabulary modeling rather than a universally optimal granularity.

original_abstract: While cutting-edge image captioning systems are increasingly describing an image coherently and exactly, recent progresses in continual learning allow deep learning systems to avoid catastrophic forgetting. However, the domain where image captioning working with continual learning is not exploited yet. We define the task in which we consolidate continual learning and image captioning as continual image captioning. In this work, we propose ContCap, a framework continually generating captions over a series of new tasks coming, seamlessly integrating continual learning into image captioning accompanied by tackling catastrophic forgetting. After proving catastrophic forgetting in image captioning, we employ freezing, knowledge distillation, and pseudo-labeling techniques to overcome the forgetting dilemma with the baseline is a simple fine-tuning scheme. We split MS-COCO 2014 dataset to perform experiments on incremental tasks without revisiting dataset of previously provided tasks. The experiments are designed to increase the degree of catastrophic forgetting and appraise the capacity of approaches. Experimental results show remarkable improvements in the performance on the old tasks, while the figure for the new task remains almost the same compared to fine-tuning. For example, pseudo-labeling increases CIDEr from 0.287 to 0.576 on the old task and 0.686 down to 0.657 BLEU1 on the new task.
generated_abstract: Modern image-captioning models achieve strong performance by jointly learning visual representations and language generation from large static corpora, but updating them as new visual concepts arrive can overwrite previously learned words and descriptions. This paper formulates image captioning as a continual, class-incremental problem and studies learning without access to the original images or captions. Building on convolutional and detector-grounded captioning architectures, and on distillation-, rehearsal-, and regularization-based classifiers, it departs from recognition-only methods by preserving a generative sequence model while expanding its visual vocabulary. We propose an end-to-end incremental training procedure that uses the previously learned captioner as a teacher, distills its token distributions and visual representations on new images, and combines these constraints with likelihood training for newly introduced concepts; optional exemplars are used when available. Experiments on staged COCO and related splits show that the method retains captioning quality and old vocabulary substantially better than naïve fine-tuning and competitive rehearsal baselines, while acquiring new concepts with modest loss in fluency. These results demonstrate that continual learning can extend grounded language generation under realistic data-retention constraints.

original_abstract: Recent advancements in machine learning research, i.e., deep learning, introduced methods that excel conventional algorithms as well as humans in several complex tasks, ranging from detection of objects in images and speech recognition to playing difficult strategic games. However, the current methodology of machine learning research and consequently, implementations of the real-world applications of such algorithms, seems to have a recurring HARKing (Hypothesizing After the Results are Known) issue. In this work, we elaborate on the algorithmic, economic and social reasons and consequences of this phenomenon. We present examples from current common practices of conducting machine learning research (e.g. avoidance of reporting negative results) and failure of generalization ability of the proposed algorithms and datasets in actual real-life usage. Furthermore, a potential future trajectory of machine learning research and development from the perspective of accountable, unbiased, ethical and privacy-aware algorithmic decision making is discussed. We would like to emphasize that with this discussion we neither claim to provide an exhaustive argumentation nor blame any specific institution or individual on the raised issues. This is simply a discussion put forth by us, insiders of the machine learning field, reflecting on us.
generated_abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) promises to replace laborious hand design with automated discovery, yet reported gains are difficult to interpret because methods differ in search spaces, training budgets, evaluation protocols, and often reuse benchmark test sets. This paper presents a systematic, reproducible empirical study of NAS rather than another search heuristic. Building on reinforcement-learning, evolutionary, sequential model-based, and weight-sharing approaches, it evaluates their search behavior against carefully matched random-search and early-stopping baselines, separating the quality of the search policy from the eventual performance of a selected model. It further examines run-to-run variability, computational cost, candidate-ranking fidelity, and performance on genuinely unseen data. The study provides a standardized benchmark and reporting protocol, together with released implementations and configurations, to make comparisons repeatable. Across conventional CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-style settings, sophisticated NAS procedures frequently offer little advantage over well-tuned random search, while weight sharing can distort rankings and benchmark reuse can exaggerate progress. The results argue that future NAS research should prioritize transparent search-phase evaluation, robust generalization, and reproducibility over isolated state-of-the-art accuracy claims.

original_abstract: One of the primary challenges faced by deep learning is the degree to which current methods exploit superficial statistics and dataset bias, rather than learning to generalise over the specific representations they have experienced. This is a critical concern because generalisation enables robust reasoning over unseen data, whereas leveraging superficial statistics is fragile to even small changes in data distribution. To illuminate the issue and drive progress towards a solution, we propose a test that explicitly evaluates abstract reasoning over visual data. We introduce a large-scale benchmark of visual questions that involve operations fundamental to many high-level vision tasks, such as comparisons of counts and logical operations on complex visual properties. The benchmark directly measures a method's ability to infer high-level relationships and to generalise them over image-based concepts. It includes multiple training/test splits that require controlled levels of generalization. We evaluate a range of deep learning architectures, and find that existing models, including those popular for vision-and-language tasks, are unable to solve seemingly-simple instances. Models using relational networks fare better but leave substantial room for improvement.
generated_abstract: Visual question answering (VQA) has advanced rapidly, yet existing benchmarks often contain strong language and dataset biases, provide limited linguistic and visual diversity, and allow models to succeed without genuine reasoning. We introduce GQA, a new dataset and benchmark for real-world visual reasoning and compositional question answering. Built from images and scene graphs in Visual Genome, GQA contains more than 22 million questions, each paired with a structured functional program that specifies its reasoning steps. Unlike earlier VQA datasets, it emphasizes balanced answer distributions, compositional language, and questions requiring multi-step operations such as querying attributes, relating objects, and comparing quantities. We further propose evaluation metrics that measure not only answer accuracy but also consistency, validity, and the ability to ground answers in relevant image regions. Experiments with strong attention, modular, and recurrent baselines reveal substantial shortcomings: contemporary systems exploit superficial correlations and struggle with compositional reasoning, despite performing well on conventional VQA benchmarks. GQA therefore exposes a larger gap between machine and human performance and provides a diagnostic foundation for developing more interpretable and genuinely reasoning-capable vision-and-language models.

original_abstract: In this paper, we propose a Dual Focal Loss (DFL) function, as a replacement for the standard cross entropy (CE) function to achieve a better treatment of the unbalanced classes in a dataset. Our DFL method is an improvement on the recently reported Focal Loss (FL) cross-entropy function, which proposes a scaling method that puts more weight on the examples that are difficult to classify over those that are easy. However, the scaling parameter of FL is empirically set, which is problem-dependent. In addition, like other CE variants, FL only focuses on the loss of true classes. Therefore, no loss feedback is gained from the false classes. Although focusing only on true examples increases probability on true classes and correspondingly reduces probability on false classes due to the nature of the softmax function, it does not achieve the best convergence due to avoidance of the loss on false classes. Our DFL method improves on the simple FL in two ways. Firstly, it takes the idea of FL to focus more on difficult examples than the easy ones, but evaluates loss on both true and negative classes with equal importance. Secondly, the scaling parameter of DFL has been made learnable so that it can tune itself by backpropagation rather than being dependent on manual tuning. In this way, our proposed DFL method offers an auto-tunable loss function that can reduce the class imbalance effect as well as put more focus on both true difficult examples and negative easy examples. Experimental results show that our proposed method provides better accuracy in every test run conducted over a variety of different network models and datasets.
generated_abstract: Accurate and efficient delineation of brain tumors in multimodal magnetic resonance images remains challenging because tumors exhibit substantial variation in size, shape, location, and appearance, while tumor pixels are severely underrepresented relative to healthy tissue. Building on fully convolutional networks, U-Net, and earlier brain-tumor CNNs, this work investigates an encoder–decoder framework that combines deep contextual representations with precise boundary recovery. Residual learning and atrous convolutions are adopted to increase the effective receptive field without excessive computational cost, while skip connections and a refined decoder preserve fine spatial detail. In contrast to conventional cross-entropy training, the method incorporates an imbalance-aware objective inspired by hierarchical Dice and loss max-pooling formulations, emphasizing difficult and under-segmented tumor regions. Multi-scale side information, motivated by holistically nested edge detection, is further used to improve boundary localization. The resulting model is trained end-to-end and evaluated on the BRATS brain-tumor benchmark using Dice, intersection-over-union, precision, and recall. Experiments show that the proposed architecture produces more accurate whole-tumor and subregion masks than standard FCN and U-Net baselines, while maintaining practical inference efficiency, demonstrating the value of jointly optimizing contextual modeling, boundary refinement, and class-imbalance handling.

original_abstract: Given an artistic portrait, recovering the latent photorealistic face that preserves the subject’s identity is challenging because the facial details are often distorted or fully lost in artistic portraits. We develop an Identity-preserving Face Recovery from Portraits method that utilizes a Style Removal network (SRN) and a Discriminative Network (DN). Our SRN, composed of an autoencoder with residual block-embedded skip connections, is designed to transfer feature maps of stylized images to the feature maps of the corresponding photorealistic faces. Owing to the Spatial Transformer Network, SRN automatically compensates for misalignments of stylized portraits to output aligned realistic face images. To ensure the identity preservation, we promote the recovered and ground truth faces to share similar visual features via a distance measure which compares features of recovered and ground truth faces extracted from a pre-trained FaceNet network. DN has multiple convolutional and fully-connected layers, and its role is to enforce recovered faces to be similar to authentic faces. Thus, we can recover high-quality photorealistic faces from unaligned portraits while preserving the identity of the face in an image. By conducting extensive evaluations on a large-scale synthesized dataset and a hand-drawn sketch dataset, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior face recovery and attains state-of-the-art results. In addition, our method can recover photorealistic faces from unseen stylized portraits, artistic paintings, and hand-drawn sketches.
generated_abstract: Neural style transfer can produce compelling images, but optimization-based methods are computationally expensive, while feed-forward alternatives are generally trained for a fixed collection of styles or sacrifice fidelity, diversity, and user control. Building on perceptual losses, texture-statistics models, and recent normalization-based approaches such as adaptive instance normalization, this paper proposes a universal style-transfer framework that operates on arbitrary content–style pairs without retraining. Its central contribution is a feature transformation that directly replaces the content feature statistics with those of the style image. Specifically, a whitening-and-coloring transform decorrelates content activations and reintroduces the style covariance, thereby transferring richer feature distributions than matching channel-wise means and variances alone. The method is embedded in a multilevel encoder–decoder pipeline, allowing coarse structures and fine textures to be stylized progressively, while interpolation and blending provide practical control over stylization strength. Experiments across diverse photographs and artworks show that the approach produces visually faithful, high-quality results for previously unseen styles, substantially faster than iterative optimization. The results demonstrate that explicit transformations in deep feature space offer an effective compromise between generality, quality, and efficiency.

original_abstract: Quantization of neural networks has become common practice, driven by the need for efficient implementations of deep neural networks on embedded devices. In this paper, we exploit an oft-overlooked degree of freedom in most networks - for a given layer, individual output channels can be scaled by any factor provided that the corresponding weights of the next layer are inversely scaled. Therefore, a given network has many factorizations which change the weights of the network without changing its function. We present a conceptually simple and easy to implement method that uses this property and show that proper factorizations significantly decrease the degradation caused by quantization. We show improvement on a wide variety of networks and achieve state-of-the-art degradation results for MobileNets. While our focus is on quantization, this type of factorization is applicable to other domains such as network-pruning, neural nets regularization and network interpretability.
generated_abstract: Deep neural networks achieve excellent accuracy, but their computation, memory footprint, and energy demands hinder deployment on mobile, embedded, and accelerator-based platforms. This paper surveys neural-network quantization as a means of reducing these costs, reviewing approaches that represent weights, activations, gradients, and intermediate computations with reduced-precision integers, fixed-point values, powers of two, or binary and ternary codes. It organizes prior work along several dimensions, including post-training versus quantization-aware training, uniform versus nonuniform and layer-wise versus channel-wise scaling, calibration and clipping strategies, incremental retraining, and hardware-supported arithmetic. In contrast to methods focused solely on weight compression or a particular accelerator, the survey relates algorithmic choices to accuracy, latency, storage, and energy trade-offs across classification and detection models. It further examines the distinct requirements of inference and training, emphasizing that stochastic rounding, range calibration, batch normalization, and selective higher-precision operations can be critical at very low bit widths. The reviewed evidence indicates that 8-bit integer inference is broadly practical with minimal accuracy loss, while 4-bit and lower precision remain architecture- and task-dependent, motivating hardware–algorithm co-design and standardized evaluation.

original_abstract: We propose a planning and perception mechanism for a robot (agent), that can only observe the underlying environment partially, in order to solve an image classification problem. A three-layer architecture is suggested that consists of a meta-layer that decides the intermediate goals, an action-layer that selects local actions as the agent navigates towards a goal, and a classification-layer that evaluates the reward and makes a prediction. We design and implement these layers using deep reinforcement learning. A generalized policy gradient algorithm is utilized to learn the parameters of these layers to maximize the expected reward. Our proposed methodology is tested on the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, which provides us with a level of explainability while interpreting the agent's intermediate goals and course of action.
generated_abstract: We address visual classification when an agent, or a team of agents, can observe only limited portions of an image and must decide where to look before producing a label. Existing multi-agent classification methods learn decentralized beliefs and consensus policies, but generally use fixed observation strategies; deep convolutional architectures improve representation quality without addressing active information acquisition. Likewise, hierarchical reinforcement learning and intrinsic motivation support exploration, while goal reasoning enables agents to select objectives, but these ideas have not been integrated with visually guided cooperative classification. We propose a goal-directed, hierarchical multi-agent deep-reinforcement-learning framework in which agents select temporally extended observation goals, attend to salient regions, exchange local beliefs, and aggregate them through decentralized consensus. A residual or densely connected convolutional encoder, augmented with local nonlinear feature modeling, extracts discriminative representations from partial observations. Saliency cues guide initial exploration, while intrinsic rewards encourage informative, nonredundant views. Experiments on image-classification tasks show that the proposed agents achieve higher accuracy with fewer observations and improved robustness to occlusion and restricted viewpoints than fixed-policy and nonhierarchical baselines. The results indicate that explicit goal selection and attention substantially improve cooperative visual reasoning.

original_abstract: While adversarial games have been well studied in various board games and electronic sports games, etc., such adversarial games remain a nearly blank field in natural language processing. As natural language is inherently an interactive game, we propose a challenging pragmatics game called Adversarial Taboo, in which an attacker and a defender compete with each other through sequential natural language interactions. The attacker is tasked with inducing the defender to speak a target word invisible to the defender, while the defender is tasked with detecting the target word before being induced by the attacker. In Adversarial Taboo, a successful attacker must hide its intention and subtly induce the defender, while a competitive defender must be cautious with its utterances and infer the intention of the attacker. To instantiate the game, we create a game environment and a competition platform. Sufficient pilot experiments and empirical studies on several baseline attack and defense strategies show promising and interesting results. Based on the analysis on the game and experiments, we discuss multiple promising directions for future research.
generated_abstract: Recent progress in neural dialogue generation and multi-agent learning has produced systems that communicate successfully in open-domain, goal-oriented, and cooperative settings. However, these approaches are often studied in isolation: end-to-end dialogue models optimize linguistic likelihood, while emergent-communication agents optimize task reward through arbitrary discrete codes. This paper reviews and organizes 80 studies spanning neural conversation, negotiation, pragmatic reasoning, knowledge grounding, and language games, identifying the assumptions that separate these traditions. It introduces a unified framework for analyzing communicative agents according to their environment, information structure, learning objective, channel constraints, and evaluation criteria, and proposes guidelines for measuring task success alongside interpretability, compositionality, generalization, and human compatibility. Unlike prior work that treats successful coordination or fluent responses as sufficient evidence of communication, the framework emphasizes the interaction between strategic reasoning, grounding, and language structure. The analysis shows that communication can emerge reliably under shared goals, but learned protocols are frequently brittle, non-compositional, and difficult for humans to understand. Pragmatic modeling, structured knowledge, planning, and interaction with human-like constraints offer promising routes toward robust, natural, and mutually intelligible communication.

original_abstract: This paper presents a new model for visual dialog, Recurrent Dual Attention Network (ReDAN), using multi-step reasoning to answer a series of questions about an image. In each question-answering turn of a dialog, ReDAN infers the answer progressively through multiple reasoning steps. In each step of the reasoning process, the semantic representation of the question is updated based on the image and the previous dialog history, and the recurrently-refined representation is used for further reasoning in the subsequent step. On the VisDial v1.0 dataset, the proposed ReDAN model achieves a new state-of-the-art of 64.47% NDCG score. Visualization on the reasoning process further demonstrates that ReDAN can locate context-relevant visual and textual clues via iterative refinement, which can lead to the correct answer step-by-step.
generated_abstract: Visual dialog requires an agent to answer questions about an image while maintaining coherence with preceding exchanges and resolving references to previously discussed objects. Existing systems extend visual question answering with recurrent history encoders, memory networks, or spatial attention, but often treat question, dialog history, image, and candidate answer as loosely coupled inputs. Consequently, they may identify relevant regions without fully exploiting conversational context, or rank answers without modeling their joint compatibility with visual evidence and the dialogue. We propose an attention-based visual dialog framework that first represents the question in the context of the dialog history, then grounds this representation in image regions through explicit visual attention, and finally evaluates candidate answers using a joint image–question–history representation. Unlike stacked or memory-based attention methods that primarily retrieve visual clues, and unlike adversarial generative approaches that emphasize response fluency, our model focuses on structured multimodal matching and answer discrimination. Experiments on the VisDial benchmarks show consistent improvements over established encoder–decoder, memory, dual-attention, and answer-synergistic baselines. Qualitative analyses further indicate more accurate reference resolution and interpretable grounding, demonstrating that jointly modeling conversational and visual evidence is essential for robust visual dialog.

original_abstract: Retrieve-and-edit based approaches to structured prediction, where structures associated with retrieved neighbors are edited to form new structures, have recently attracted increased interest. However, much recent work merely conditions on retrieved structures (e.g., in a sequence-to-sequence framework), rather than explicitly manipulating them. We show we can perform accurate sequence labeling by explicitly (and only) copying labels from retrieved neighbors. Moreover, because this copying is label-agnostic, we can achieve impressive performance in zero-shot sequence-labeling tasks. We additionally consider a dynamic programming approach to sequence labeling in the presence of retrieved neighbors, which allows for controlling the number of distinct (copied) segments used to form a prediction, and leads to both more interpretable and accurate predictions.
generated_abstract: Sequence tagging systems have achieved strong results with bidirectional recurrent networks, character representations, and conditional random fields, but their performance often deteriorates when labeled data are scarce or the target domain and language differ from training conditions. Existing transfer-learning approaches address this limitation through recurrent hierarchies or auxiliary tasks, while contextual representations such as CoVe, ELMo, and BERT provide richer lexical and syntactic information but are not designed specifically for structured tagging decisions. This paper proposes a unified transfer-learning architecture for low-resource sequence labeling that combines a pre-trained bidirectional Transformer with subword representations and a CRF decoding layer. Unlike earlier BiLSTM-CNN models, the proposed system replaces recurrent encoding with self-attention and fine-tunes contextual representations jointly with the tagger; unlike conventional feature-based or cross-lingual methods, it requires no gazetteers, parallel corpora, or manually designed linguistic features. Experiments across named entity recognition and part-of-speech tagging datasets, including out-of-domain and low-resource settings, show consistent improvements over recurrent, static-embedding, and non-contextual baselines. The results demonstrate that pretrained bidirectional representations substantially improve transferability, while structured decoding remains valuable for enforcing globally coherent label sequences.

original_abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of how and why face recognition accuracy differs between men and women. We show that accuracy is lower for women due to the combination of (1) the impostor distribution for women having a skew toward higher similarity scores, and (2) the genuine distribution for women having a skew toward lower similarity scores. We show that this phenomenon of the impostor and genuine distributions for women shifting closer towards each other is general across datasets of African-American, Caucasian, and Asian faces. We show that the distribution of facial expressions may differ between male/female, but that the accuracy difference persists for image subsets rated confidently as neutral expression. The accuracy difference also persists for image subsets rated as close to zero pitch angle. Even when removing images with forehead partially occluded by hair/hat, the same impostor/genuine accuracy difference persists. We show that the female genuine distribution improves when only female images without facial cosmetics are used, but that the female impostor distribution also degrades at the same time. Lastly, we show that the accuracy difference persists even if a state-of-the-art deep learning method is trained from scratch using training data explicitly balanced between male and female images and subjects.
generated_abstract: Deep face recognition systems achieve near-saturated performance on conventional benchmarks, yet their behavior across demographic and appearance covariates remains poorly understood. Building on angular- and cosine-margin losses, large-scale datasets such as MS-Celeb-1M and VGGFace2, and prior analyses of pose, age, and skin-tone effects, this paper conducts a controlled empirical study of modern face matchers under unconstrained conditions. Rather than introducing another loss function or training corpus, we propose an evaluation framework that separates genuine-match degradation from impostor-score shifts and measures performance across age, gender, pose, illumination, and occlusion. We train and compare contemporary convolutional models with normalized angular objectives, evaluate them on public verification and identification protocols, and examine whether additional or demographic-balanced training data mitigate observed disparities. Results show that aggregate accuracy can conceal substantial subgroup variation: covariates affect impostor and genuine distributions differently, and balancing data or fine-tuning on underrepresented groups does not uniformly improve performance. In particular, age-related errors are driven primarily by increased impostor similarity. The findings demonstrate the need for covariate-aware evaluation and caution against interpreting benchmark-level gains as equitable recognition performance.

original_abstract: We propose an unsupervised strategy for the selection of justification sentences for multi-hop question answering (QA) that (a) maximizes the relevance of the selected sentences, (b) minimizes the overlap between the selected facts, and (c) maximizes the coverage of both question and answer. This unsupervised sentence selection method can be coupled with any supervised QA approach. We show that the sentences selected by our method improve the performance of a state-of-the-art supervised QA model on two multi-hop QA datasets: AI2's Reasoning Challenge (ARC) and Multi-Sentence Reading Comprehension (MultiRC). We obtain new state-of-the-art performance on both datasets among approaches that do not use external resources for training the QA system: 56.82\% F1 on ARC (41.24\% on Challenge and 64.49\% on Easy) and 26.1\% EM0 on MultiRC. Our justification sentences have higher quality than the justifications selected by a strong information retrieval baseline, e.g., by 5.4\% F1 in MultiRC. We also show that our unsupervised selection of justification sentences is more stable across domains than a state-of-the-art supervised sentence selection method.
generated_abstract: Open-domain question answering systems have made substantial progress in extracting answers from individual passages, yet they remain unreliable when answering requires locating, combining, and comparing evidence distributed across documents. Existing multi-hop datasets expose this limitation, while prior solutions address it through passage reranking, cross-passage verification, entailment transfer, or graph convolution over entity mentions; these approaches either assume relevant documents are available, aggregate evidence only indirectly, or provide limited supervision for identifying the reasoning path. We propose an evidence-aware multi-hop question answering framework that jointly selects relevant documents and sentences, represents their entities and relations in a cross-document graph, and performs iterative reasoning before predicting the answer. Unlike independent extractive readers, the model explicitly links supporting facts and uses their accumulated representation to suppress distractors and resolve competing answer candidates. We evaluate the framework on established multi-document and multi-sentence benchmarks, including WikiHop and HotpotQA, under realistic retrieval settings. Results show consistent gains over strong retrieval, reading-comprehension, reranking, and graph-based baselines, while predicted supporting facts improve interpretability. Ablation studies confirm that both evidence selection and cross-document reasoning are essential.
